correction: The IRS FY 2021 annual report gives $3.5 billion as its Criminal Investigation crypto-seizure total, 93% of all CI seizures. Its cases include the Silk Road funds seized on 3 November 2020, valued at more than $1 billion the next day, before the submission’s own 2021 start date for Hidden Treasure. The later primary TIGTA audit distinguishes Hidden Treasure’s tools/training project from aggregate criminal-enforcement activity. Its benefits cannot be relabelled as the whole FY 2021 seizure total or a measured programme ROI.
effect: Removes the claimed quantified American programme result used to make the proposed German resource expansion appear rapidly self-financing. The actual IRS seizure achievements remain real.
limits: This does not show that the requested German technology investment or staffing is unnecessary, that blockchain-analysis tools fail, that Hidden Treasure produced no benefits, or that no part of the IRS total involved related tools. TIGTA explicitly recognises real criminal uses of those tools. No actual alternative ROI is calculated. Missing programme accounts alone are not treated as proof of an error, and no intent is inferred.
context_and_alternatives: All seven submission pages were read. Pages 4–5 present several international technology examples, page 5 requests resources, and page 6 explicitly uses the American programme’s alleged ROI to support financing. The error is not inferred merely from a disagreement with the proposed budget.

The strongest benign reading is that the operation name is loose shorthand for the wider, multi-year IRS crypto-enforcement strategy described in the following paragraph. That can explain the prose, but does not rescue the attribution of the entire annual result to a 2021 operation or the later programme-specific ROI claim.
November 2020 falls within the United States FY 2021: it is not a calendar-year versus fiscal-year mistake in the primary report. The contradiction is the operation’s causal attribution and scope.

TIGTA’s 2024 audit reports license acquisition beginning in December 2020, expressly before and during Hidden Treasure. It found no specific enforcement deliverables or written summary accounts of project effectiveness, while also explaining that acquired tools were used in real cases. Its relevant section, methodology and agency response were checked. The finding does not equate lack of written accounts with zero outcomes.

The exact addressed BT 21/1937 is dated 1 October 2025. Its cover, reporting framework and cost sections were checked; the original bill’s federal resource estimates are not replaced by the later enacted law. No claim that the bill itself introduces a new tax is made.

Seizure valuations are not by themselves an identified measure of additional tax receipts. The submission gives no explicit cost-base calculation connecting the annual aggregate to a specific programme. This is an additional limit on the stated fiscal inference, not a separate issue or a replacement estimate.
materiality_explanation: Major: the named programme’s purported billion-dollar result and more-than-fiftyfold return are directly used as the financing precedent for a €50 million investment and 500 posts. Moving the numerator back to agency-wide seizures removes that quantitative programme-success precedent. This judgment is separate from whether the requested resources are good policy.
direction_explanation: True: attributing the whole large seizure total and an exceptional ROI to the named intervention strengthens the author’s explicit argument for a similarly funded German technology and staffing expansion.

confidence.text_source_mismatch: high for the aggregate-versus-programme attribution and pre-operation seizure; no precise true ROI asserted
